crossref.title: Random sample consensus
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>A new paradigm, Random Sample Consensus (RANSAC), for fitting a model to experimental data is introduced. RANSAC is capable of interpreting/smoothing data containing a significant percentage of gross errors, and is thus ideally suited for applications in automated image analysis where interpretation is based on the data provided by error-prone feature detectors. A major portion of this paper describes the application of RANSAC to the Location Determination Problem (LDP): Given an image depicting a set of landmarks with known locations, determine that point in space from which the image was obtained. In response to a RANSAC requirement, new results are derived on the minimum number of landmarks needed to obtain a solution, and algorithms are presented for computing these minimum-landmark solutions in closed form. These results provide the basis for an automatic system that can solve the LDP under difficult viewing</jats:p>

In complex multi-target scenarios, maintaining robustness with KF often requires computationally expensive mechanisms like JPDA or MHT. 41,42 Therefore, for non-real-time reconstruction pursuing ultimate precision, Geometry-& Density-Based methods (such as DBSCAN 29,43–48 combined with RANSAC 49–51 ) offer a more robust paradigm by identifying noise based on density and bridging trajectory gaps through geometric consistency rather than motion priors.

The RANSAC algorithm 49 is inherently robust against outliers in the data (caused by residual localization jitter or minor false positives), ensuring that the fitted trajectory lines possess high smoothness and stability.

This part will first showcase the algorithm’s entire process, from raw signal input, through Stage 1 (high-precision point cloud localization), Stage 2 (DBSCAN denoising and separation), to the final Stage (RANSAC robust fitting).

Trajectory Integrity and Repair: Through the integration of DBSCAN and RANSAC, the algorithm pipeline not only effectively removes isolated noise points and achieves automatic separation of multi-vehicle trajectories, but its tailored collinear cluster merging mechanism also successfully repairs the topological discontinuities of trajectories caused by intermittent signal loss.
As shown in Figure 7(d), the RANSAC algorithm successfully ignores the residual noise points (id: -1) from (c) and linearly reconstructs the valid clusters.

To further refine trajectories and address the common problem of trajectory fragmentation in DAS data—often caused by signal intermittence or overly strict filtering rules of DBSCAN clustering—we introduce linear fitting based on Random Sample Consensus (RANSAC) and design a collinear cluster merging mechanism: RANSAC Fitting: Given that vehicles are generally expected to maintain constant velocity in typical scenarios (appearing as linear trajectories on the spatio-temporal map), we apply the RANSACRegressor for straight-line fitting to each DBSCAN cluster.
Finally, we apply the RANSAC algorithm 49 to the individual clean trajectory point clusters generated in stage (c) for robust straight-line fitting.
